lessons.title: Investing Is Not Speculating
lessons.key_idea: Graham defines investing as an operation that, after careful analysis, promises safety of your money and a fair return, and anything else is speculation.

lessons.title: Meet Your Moody Partner, Mr. Market
lessons.key_idea: The market is like an emotional business partner who offers you a different price every day, and you should take advantage of his moods rather than be ruled by them.

lessons.title: Your Worst Enemy Is You
lessons.key_idea: Success in investing depends far more on emotional discipline than on intelligence, because fear and greed drive people to buy high and sell low.

lessons.title: Defensive or Enterprising: Pick Your Path
lessons.key_idea: What separates the two types of investor is how much time and effort you are willing to put in, not how much risk you take.

lessons.title: Balancing Stocks and Bonds
lessons.key_idea: Graham suggests keeping between 25 and 75 percent in stocks, often starting at an even split, and rebalancing to stay steady as markets swing.

lessons.title: Buy a Business, Not a Ticker
lessons.key_idea: A share is a piece of a real company, so judge it by its size, financial strength, steady earnings, dividend history, and a sensible price compared with earnings.

lessons.title: The Margin of Safety
lessons.key_idea: Graham's central idea is to buy only when the price sits well below a business's true value, leaving a cushion that protects you from mistakes and bad luck.

plan.title: The Intelligent Investor
plan.author: Benjamin Graham
plan.confidence_note: I know this classic's core arguments well, including investment versus speculation, Mr. Market, the defensive and enterprising investor, and margin of safety, though exact figures vary between editions.
plan.one_liner: The calm, common-sense rulebook for investing that has quietly guided smart money for over 70 years.
plan.summary: First published in 1949 and revised several times, The Intelligent Investor is Benjamin Graham's guide to investing sensibly without needing genius or luck. Graham draws a firm line between investing, which rests on careful analysis and protecting your money, and speculating, which is betting on price moves. He argues that the biggest danger to most investors is not the market but their own emotions. Through his famous character Mr. Market, he shows how to treat wild price swings as opportunities rather than orders. He explains how to split money between stocks and bonds, how to choose an approach that matches the effort you can give, and how to judge a company as a real business. Everything rests on one principle: always buy with a margin of safety.
